content: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) can lead to significant health complications, including an increased risk of acquiring HIV. Beyond health, STIs also have profound social and economic consequences. Certain STIs, such as herpes simplex virus (HSV) and syphilis, disproportionately affect women and newborns. For instance, if a woman contracts primary HSV during the third trimester of pregnancy, it can result in congenital herpes, which may lead to neurocognitive impairments, developmental delays, or even infant mortality. Similarly, congenital syphilis can cause severe morbidity or death in infants. The clinical presentation of genital ulcer disease poses a diagnostic challenge for healthcare providers, as it can be caused by both STI-related and non-STI-related factors. Despite the presence of genital ulcers, many individuals continue to engage in sexual activity, which underscores the importance of timely diagnosis and treatment to reduce the transmission of STIs and HIV. A systematic review conducted up to September 2019 evaluated the sensitivity and specificity of syndromic management approaches for diagnosing multiple STIs associated with anogenital ulcers. However, no studies were found on detecting lymphogranuloma venereum. For herpes detection based on clinical diagnosis, 15 studies provided 20 pooled estimates, while for syphilis detection in individuals with genital ulcer disease, 15 studies provided 22 pooled estimates. The global distribution, incidence, and prevalence of the pathogens causing genital ulcer disease vary significantly by geographic region and population subgroup, which affects the predictive value of diagnostic tests. The accuracy of syndromic management depends on factors such as the clinician's skill and experience, the clinical setting (e.g., STI centers versus primary care), and patient characteristics. Predictive values for tests may be lower among general populations with a lower prevalence of STIs. Notably, there is no significant difference in the causative agents of genital ulcer disease between individuals living with HIV and those without HIV. The desirable effects of syndromic management include appropriate treatment, cure, reduced STI and HIV transmission, and partner notification. However, undesirable effects, such as missed cases, inappropriate treatment, antimicrobial resistance, and stigma, must also be considered. Over-treatment may be acceptable in high-morbidity settings to control undetected cases, such as syphilis, but it carries risks of unnecessary treatment and stigma due to low specificity. The cost-effectiveness of syndromic management varies. While it may be cost-saving in resource-limited settings, such as rural South Africa, the costs of missed cases with syndromic management make treating all cases more cost-effective in some scenarios. Syndromic management has been implemented with varying success in many lowand middle-income countries, but challenges remain, including inadequate training, suboptimal management, and limited access to diagnostic tools. Training and supervision are critical for scaling up syndromic management.
